summary.title: Against 3X Speed
summary.one_liner: Fast consumption of audiobooks and lectures creates an illusion of knowledge; durable learning comes from slower reflection, writing, spaced repetition and direct experience.
keywords: water in a cup theory of learning
is listening to audiobooks fast good for retention
takeaways: Listening to audiobooks at 3x speed is a poor way to retain information; spaced repetition and deep processing work better.
The 'Water in a Cup' model of learning (pouring information into minds) creates an illusion of knowledge, especially when rushed.
Writing in your own words and revisiting ideas act as spaced repetition and help consolidate memory.
Direct experience and immersion, such as language immersion, reveal knowledge that lectures and books cannot.
It is fine not to know everything; build expertise slowly and deliberately rather than measuring learning by consumption volume.
summary.summary: This is a personal essay by David Perell arguing against consuming information at high speed. He uses a character named Mike, who listens to audiobooks at 3x speed, to illustrate what he calls the 'Water in a Cup' model of learning, and he critiques lecture-based schooling, citing a study on attention spans, Sal Khan's Louisiana Purchase example, and the history of US education standardization. The essay contrasts this with learning through writing, spaced repetition, and direct experience, using anecdotes from travel in Europe and Oaxaca and his college professor's conversation-based class. It ends with a suggestion that Mike slow down and learn at a human pace, keeping audiobook speed modest for dense books.
